Spin is not a conserved quantity of the free Dirac Hamiltonian, but its component along the momentum is. The
definition below names this component, following @pal2011majorana [Sec. 4.1].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-dq-helicity}
#### Helicity

The **spin operator** of the Dirac theory is $\vec S = \tfrac12\vec\Sigma$ with $\Sigma_k = \tfrac{i}{2}\epsilon_{kij}\gamma^i\gamma^j =
\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_k, \sigma_k)$ in both the Weyl and the Dirac representation. The **helicity** of a state of momentum
$\vec p \neq 0$ is the eigenvalue $h = \pm1$ of
$$
h(\vec p) = \vec\Sigma\cdot\hat p, \qquad \hat p = \vec p/|\vec p| ,
$$ {#eq-dq-helicity}
twice the spin along the direction of motion; $h = +1$ is called right-helical and $h = -1$ left-helical
@pal2011majorana [Sec. 4.1, eqs. (4.1)-(4.3)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The spinors of @exm-dq-z-spinors are helicity eigenstates. The first example identifies their helicities and shows how
to build helicity eigenstates in general.

::: {#exm-dq-helicity-z}
#### Helicity of the spinors

For $\vec p$ along $+z$, $h = \Sigma_3$, so $u^\uparrow$ has $h = +1$ and $u^\downarrow$ has $h = -1$. For a general direction, choosing
$\xi$ as an eigenvector of $\vec\sigma\cdot\hat p$ with eigenvalue $h$ makes $u(p)$ an eigenvector of $h(\vec p)$ with the
same eigenvalue, because $\sqrt{p\cdot\sigma} = \sqrt{E - h|\vec p|}$ on such $\xi$ is a number: $u = (\sqrt{E - h|\vec
p|}\,\xi, \sqrt{E + h|\vec p|}\,\xi)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Helicity is conserved for a free particle but depends on the observer. The second example gives both facts, with the
argument of @pal2011majorana [Sec. 4.1].

::: {#exm-dq-helicity-frame}
#### Conserved but not invariant

$[H, \vec\Sigma\cdot\vec p] = 0$, so helicity is a constant of the free motion (@exr-dq-helicity-commute). But an observer
moving along $\hat p$ faster than a massive particle sees its momentum reversed while its spin, a component of the
antisymmetric tensor $M^{ij}$ transverse to the boost, is unchanged: the helicity flips. Only for $m = 0$, where no observer
overtakes the particle, is helicity Lorentz invariant.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Without mass helicity and chirality coincide on positive-energy states. The third example shows this from the Weyl
form of the Hamiltonian, anticipating @prp-dq-chirality-helicity.

::: {#exm-dq-helicity-massless}
#### Massless particles

For $m = 0$, $H = \operatorname{diag}(-\vec\sigma\cdot\vec p, \vec\sigma\cdot\vec p)$ (@exm-dq-weyl-alpha). A positive-energy
right-handed state $(0, \chi)$ has $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec p\chi = |\vec p|\chi$, so $h = +1$; a positive-energy left-handed state
$(\chi, 0)$ has $-\vec\sigma\cdot\vec p\chi = |\vec p|\chi$, so $h = -1$. For massless fermions chirality is helicity, and for
negative energies the relation is reversed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the relevant commutators. It shows which angular momentum is conserved and why helicity
survives although the spin does not.

::: {#exr-dq-helicity-commute}
#### What commutes with $H$

For the free $H$, show that $[H, \Sigma_3] \neq 0$ when $\vec p$ is not along $z$, that $[H, \vec\Sigma\cdot\vec p] = 0$, and that
$\vec J = \vec L + \tfrac12\vec\Sigma$ commutes with $H$ although $\vec L = \vec x \times \vec p$ does not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Sigma_k$ commutes with $\beta$ and $[\alpha_j, \Sigma_k] = 2i\epsilon_{jkl}\alpha_l$, so $[H, \Sigma_k] = 2i\epsilon_{jkl}p_j\alpha_l = 2i(\vec
\alpha \times \vec p)_k$, non-zero unless $\vec p \parallel \hat k$. Contracting with $p_k$ gives $(\vec\alpha \times \vec p)\cdot\vec p
= 0$, so helicity commutes. $[H, L_k] = [\alpha_jp_j, \epsilon_{klm}x_lp_m] = -i\epsilon_{klm}\alpha_lp_m = -i(\vec\alpha \times \vec
p)_k$, and $[H, L_k + \tfrac12\Sigma_k] = -i(\vec\alpha \times \vec p)_k + i(\vec\alpha \times \vec p)_k = 0$: only the total angular
momentum is conserved, which is why the Dirac hydrogen atom is labelled by $j$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The eigenvector is $\xi \propto (\hat p_z + 1, \hat p_x + i\hat p_y) = (4/3, 2/3 + 2i/3)$; the spinor satisfies both

{{< sage exr-dq-helicity-eigen >}}

Pal's frame argument can be made quantitative with the rapidity. The third exercise computes the helicity seen by a
moving observer.

::: {#exr-dq-overtaking}
#### Overtaking a particle

A particle of mass $m$ moves along $+z$ with rapidity $w$ and spin up along $z$. An observer moves along $+z$ with rapidity
$w_0$. Show that the observer sees rapidity $w - w_0$ and spin still up along $z$, so the helicity is $+1$ for $w_0 < w$ and
$-1$ for $w_0 > w$. Why is no such observer available when $m = 0$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Rapidities along one axis add, so the particle has rapidity $w - w_0$ in the observer's frame and momentum $m\sinh(w -
w_0)$, negative when $w_0 > w$. The spin state $\xi^\uparrow$ is unchanged because the boost $S = \exp(-w_0S^{03})$ is diagonal
with $\xi^\uparrow$ as eigenvector in each block. So $h = \operatorname{sign}(w - w_0)$. For $m = 0$ the particle moves at the
speed of light and no observer has $w_0 > w$: its helicity is the same in all frames.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

Chirality is the eigenvalue of $\gamma_5$; it is Lorentz invariant, since $\gamma_5$ commutes with the spinor generators, but
it is not conserved. The proposition below relates it to helicity and gives its time dependence.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-dq-chirality-helicity}
#### Chirality and helicity

Let $P_{L,R} = \tfrac12(1 \mp \gamma_5)$ be the chiral projectors ($\gamma_5 = \operatorname{diag}(-1, -1, 1, 1)$ in the Weyl
representation). For a positive-energy spinor $u$ of helicity $h$,
$$
\frac{u^\dagger P_Ru}{u^\dagger u} = \frac{1 + hv}{2}, \qquad v = \frac{|\vec p|}{E} ,
$$ {#eq-dq-chiral-fraction}
so chirality equals helicity only in the limit $v \to 1$. Moreover $[H, \gamma_5] = 2m\beta\gamma_5$, so chirality is conserved
only for $m = 0$; a state that is left-handed at $t = 0$ with momentum $p$ has $\langle\gamma_5\rangle(t) = -1 + \tfrac{m^2}{E^2}(1 -
\cos 2Et)$ @pal2011majorana [Sec. 4.2].

*Proof.* By @exm-dq-helicity-z, $u = (\sqrt{E - h|\vec p|}\,\xi, \sqrt{E + h|\vec p|}\,\xi)$, so the right-handed (lower) part
has weight $E + h|\vec p|$ out of $2E$. In the Weyl representation $\alpha_k$ is block diagonal and commutes with $\gamma_5$,
while $\beta$ is off-diagonal and anticommutes, so $[H, \gamma_5] = m[\beta, \gamma_5] = 2m\beta\gamma_5$. The time dependence follows
from $e^{-iHt} = \cos Et - i(H/E)\sin Et$ (@exr-dq-hamiltonian-projector) applied to $(1, 0, 0, 0)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For electrons in accelerators the wrong-chirality admixture is tiny. The first example evaluates
@eq-dq-chiral-fraction at a typical energy. It shows how quickly helicity and chirality become interchangeable at high energy.

::: {#exm-dq-ultrarelativistic}
#### Fast electrons

For $E \gg m$, $1 - v = 1 - \sqrt{1 - m^2/E^2} \approx m^2/2E^2$, so a helicity $+1$ electron is left-handed with probability
$(1 - v)/2 \approx m^2/4E^2$. At $E = 1$ GeV with $m = 0.511$ MeV this is $6.5 \times 10^{-8}$. Couplings that act only on
left-handed fields, like the weak interaction, therefore act almost only on left-helical electrons at high energy.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A left-handed state at rest is an equal mixture of positive and negative energies, and the mass makes it oscillate.
The second example reads the oscillation off @fig-dq-helicity.

::: {#exm-dq-chirality-oscillation}
#### Chirality oscillates

At $\vec p = 0$, $\langle\gamma_5\rangle(t) = -\cos 2mt$: the state $(1, 0, 0, 0) = \tfrac12[(1, 0, 1, 0) + (1, 0, -1, 0)]$ is half a
positive-energy and half a negative-energy rest spinor, and the relative phase $e^{2imt}$ turns left into right and back
with period $\pi/m$. For $|\vec p| \gg m$ the amplitude $m^2/E^2$ is small, the right panel of @fig-dq-helicity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Helicity and chirality are separately invariant under different operations. The third example collects the
properties that distinguish them, which @pal2011majorana [Sec. 4] summarises as "opposite characteristics".

::: {#exm-dq-chirality-helicity-table}
#### Two kinds of handedness

Helicity: conserved for a free particle ($[H, h] = 0$), invariant under rotations, not under boosts (@exm-dq-helicity-frame).
Chirality: invariant under all proper Lorentz transformations ($[\gamma_5, S^{\mu\nu}] = 0$), not conserved
($[H, \gamma_5] \neq 0$). Both coincide for massless positive-energy states (@exm-dq-helicity-massless), and for massive
particles neither is a frame-independent conserved label: "left or right?" has no answer for a massive fermion.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the chiral fraction for a momentum along $z$. It shows where the factor $E \pm |\vec p|$ comes
from.

::: {#exr-dq-chirality-fraction}
#### The chiral fraction

For $u^\uparrow$ and $u^\downarrow$ of @exm-dq-z-spinors compute $u^\dagger P_Ru/u^\dagger u$ and express it in terms of $v = \tanh w$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $u^\uparrow = \sqrt m(e^{-w/2}, 0, e^{w/2}, 0)$, $u^\dagger u = m(e^{-w} + e^w)$ and $u^\dagger P_Ru = me^w$, so the fraction is
$e^w/(e^w + e^{-w}) = \tfrac12(1 + \tanh w) = \tfrac12(1 + v)$, with $h = +1$. For $u^\downarrow$ the components are exchanged and the
fraction is $\tfrac12(1 - v)$, with $h = -1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The time dependence of chirality is a computation with the matrix exponential of $H$. The second exercise performs it
with Sage, for an arbitrary momentum along $z$.

::: {#exr-dq-chirality-time}
#### Chirality in time

With Sage, compute $\psi(t) = e^{-iHt}(1, 0, 0, 0)$ for $H = p\alpha_3 + m\beta$ in the Weyl representation and simplify
$\langle\gamma_5\rangle(t)$. Check also $[H, \gamma_5] = 2m\beta\gamma_5$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Using $H^2 = E^2$, $e^{-iHt} = \cos Et - i\sin Et\,H/E$, and the result is $-1 + (m^2/E^2)(1 - \cos 2Et)$:

{{< sage exr-dq-chirality-time >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The commutator $[H, \gamma_5]$ was computed in the Weyl representation, where it is easy. The third exercise derives it in
a representation-free way.

::: {#exr-dq-gamma5-commutator}
#### The commutator without matrices

Using only $\gamma_5\gamma^\mu = -\gamma^\mu\gamma_5$, show that $\gamma_5$ commutes with $\alpha_k = \gamma^0\gamma^k$ and anticommutes with $\beta =
\gamma^0$. Deduce $[H, \gamma_5] = 2m\beta\gamma_5$ in every representation, and $[H, \gamma_5] = 0$ for $m = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\gamma_5\gamma^0\gamma^k = -\gamma^0\gamma_5\gamma^k = \gamma^0\gamma^k\gamma_5$: two anticommutations give a commutation. $\gamma_5\gamma^0 = -\gamma^0\gamma_5$
directly. Hence $[\vec\alpha\cdot\vec p, \gamma_5] = 0$ and $[\beta m, \gamma_5] = m(\beta\gamma_5 - \gamma_5\beta) = 2m\beta\gamma_5$. For $m = 0$ chirality
is conserved, and the Dirac equation splits into the Weyl equations of @def-dq-weyl-equation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
These exercises combine the spinors, the projectors and the helicity. The first builds a superposition of positive and
negative energies with Sage and finds the term that oscillates at twice the energy.

::: {#exr-dq-free-interference}
#### Interference of the two energies

For $m = 24$, $\vec p = (2, 3, 6)$, let $\psi(t, \vec x) = [u^1(\vec p)e^{-iEt} + v^1(-\vec p)e^{iEt}]e^{i\vec p\cdot\vec x}$. With Sage,
compute $\psi^\dagger\psi$ and $\psi^\dagger\alpha_3\psi$ as functions of $t$, and identify the terms oscillating as $\cos 2Et$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The density is constant, $\psi^\dagger\psi = 4E = 100$, because $u^\dagger(\vec p)v(-\vec p) = 0$ (@exr-dq-orthogonality). The current has no
constant part: the two waves carry $+12$ and $-12$, the negative-energy wave moving against its momentum
(@exr-dq-negative-energy-meaning). What remains is the interference term $j_3 = -\tfrac{4756}{49}\cos2Et$, oscillating at $2E = 50$: the
trembling motion of @prp-dq-zitterbewegung, already present in a single superposition of plane waves:

{{< sage exr-dq-free-interference >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The vector current between two different spinors splits into a convection and a spin part. The second exercise
derives this Gordon decomposition, which shows where the magnetic moment of @thm-dq-pauli-limit hides in the current.

::: {#exr-dq-gordon-decomposition}
#### Gordon decomposition

Show that $\bar u(p')\gamma^\mu u(p) = \bar u(p')\big[\frac{(p + p')^\mu}{2m} + \frac{i\sigma^{\mu\nu}(p' - p)_\nu}{2m}\big]u(p)$, with
$\sigma^{\mu\nu} = \tfrac{i}{2}[\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu]$. (Hint: write $\gamma^\mu = \frac{1}{2m}(\gamma^\mu p\!\!\!/ + p\!\!\!/'\gamma^\mu)$ between the
spinors.)
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Between $\bar u(p')$ and $u(p)$, $p\!\!\!/u = mu$ and $\bar u'p\!\!\!/' = m\bar u'$, so the hint holds. Now $\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu =
\eta^{\mu\nu} - i\sigma^{\mu\nu}$ and $\gamma^\nu\gamma^\mu = \eta^{\mu\nu} + i\sigma^{\mu\nu}$, hence $\gamma^\mu p\!\!\!/ + p\!\!\!/'\gamma^\mu = (p +
p')^\mu - i\sigma^{\mu\nu}p_\nu + i\sigma^{\mu\nu}p'_\nu$, which is the claim. The first term is the current of a charged scalar; the
second, proportional to the momentum transfer, couples the spin to the field strength and gives $g = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In one dimension the spinors have two components and everything can be written in closed form. The third exercise
collects the free theory of @exm-dq-one-dimension, the theory used for the Klein step.

::: {#exr-dq-free-1d}
#### Free spinors in one dimension

For $H = \sigma_1p + \sigma_3m$, write the normalised eigenvectors $u(p)$, $v(p)$ for $\pm E$, the projectors $\tfrac12(1 \pm
H/E)$, and check $u^\dagger(p)v(p) = 0$. Compare with the normalisations of @calogeracos1999klein [eqs. (9)-(12)].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$u(p) = (E + m, p)/\sqrt{2E(E + m)}$ and $v(p) = (-p, E + m)/\sqrt{2E(E + m)}$ are orthonormal: $u^\dagger v = (-(E + m)p + p(E +
m))/2E(E + m) = 0$. The projectors are $\tfrac12(1 \pm (\sigma_1p + \sigma_3m)/E)$, and $u u^\dagger = \tfrac12(1 + H/E)$, as a direct
computation of the entries $(E + m)^2$, $(E + m)p$, $p^2$ over $2E(E + m)$ shows. @calogeracos1999klein use $\gamma^0 = \sigma_3$,
$\gamma^1 = i\sigma_1$ and the spinors $(ik, E - m)$, which are ours up to the change of basis $e^{i\pi\sigma_3/4}$ and the
normalisation over a box of length $2L$.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

## The non-relativistic limit {#sec-dirac-nonrelativistic}

An electron in an atom moves at about $Z\alpha$ times the speed of light, so its Dirac equation should reduce to a
Schrödinger equation with small corrections. This part couples the equation to an electromagnetic field, finds the
Pauli equation as the leading term with the gyromagnetic ratio $g = 2$ predicted rather than assumed, and then
organises the corrections systematically with the Foldy-Wouthuysen transformation, which produces the relativistic
kinetic energy, the spin-orbit coupling and the Darwin term, following @costella1995foldy and @eides2001hydrogen [Sec.
VII]. The Dirac representation of @exm-dq-dirac-alpha is used throughout, since in it the rest energy separates the
large from the small components.

### The Pauli equation

A charged particle couples to the electromagnetic potential by the minimal coupling $\vec p \to \vec p - q\vec A$ of
@def-emm-minimal-coupling, written covariantly as the derivative $\partial_\mu + iqA_\mu$ that the gauge-theory chapter
develops. In a uniform magnetic field the Dirac equation can be solved exactly, and its Landau
levels show the factor $g = 2$ directly, as the figure shows.

![Landau levels of a Dirac particle of charge $q$ in a uniform field $B$ ($p_z = 0$, $m = 1$): the exact levels $E_N =
\sqrt{m^2 + 2N|qB|}$ (solid) and the Pauli levels $m + N|qB|/m$ (dashed). The level $N$ contains the orbital level $N$
with spin along the field and the orbital level $N - 1$ with spin against it, a degeneracy that holds only for $g = 2$.
Generated by `figures/dq-landau.sage`.](figures/dq-landau.svg){#fig-dq-landau width=70%}

The definition below couples the Dirac equation to a potential $A^\mu = (\Phi, \vec A)$. It is the relativistic form of the
minimal coupling of a classical charge (@def-emm-minimal-coupling); the gauge-theory chapter applies the same rule to
charged scalar fields.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-dq-minimal-coupling}
#### Minimal coupling

The **Dirac equation in an electromagnetic potential** $A_\mu$ for a particle of charge $q$ is
$$
(i\gamma^\mu D_\mu - m)\psi = 0, \qquad D_\mu = \partial_\mu + iqA_\mu ,
$$ {#eq-dq-minimal-coupling}
or, in Hamiltonian form,
$$
i\partial_t\psi = \big(\vec\alpha\cdot\vec\pi + \beta m + q\Phi\big)\psi, \qquad \vec\pi = \vec p - q\vec A = -i\nabla - q\vec A ,
$$ {#eq-dq-coupled-hamiltonian}
where $A^\mu = (\Phi, \vec A)$, $\vec B = \nabla \times \vec A$ and $\vec E = -\nabla\Phi - \partial_t\vec A$. For the electron
$q = -e$ with $e > 0$ and $e^2 = 4\pi\alpha$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Coulomb field of a nucleus is the potential of the hydrogen atom. The first example writes the Hamiltonian that
@sec-dirac-hydrogen solves exactly.

::: {#exm-dq-coulomb-h}
#### The Coulomb potential

A nucleus of charge $Ze$ at the origin has $\Phi = Ze/(4\pi r)$, so an electron has potential energy $q\Phi = -Ze^2/(4\pi r) =
-Z\alpha/r$ and Hamiltonian $H = \vec\alpha\cdot\vec p + \beta m - Z\alpha/r$. The coupling enters only through the combination
$q\Phi$, so a positron in the same field sees $+Z\alpha/r$, the charge-conjugate problem of @exm-dq-c-hydrogen.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A uniform magnetic field has a potential linear in the coordinates. The second example writes the symmetric gauge used
for @fig-dq-landau.

::: {#exm-dq-uniform-b}
#### A uniform magnetic field

$\vec A = \tfrac12\vec B \times \vec x$ has $\nabla \times \vec A = \vec B$; for $\vec B = B\hat z$, $\vec A = (-By/2, Bx/2, 0)$ and
$\vec\pi = (p_x + qBy/2, p_y - qBx/2, p_z)$. The components $\pi_x, \pi_y$ do not commute, $[\pi_x, \pi_y] = iqB$
(@exr-dq-pi-commutator), so $\pi_x^2 + \pi_y^2$ is an oscillator Hamiltonian with levels $|qB|(2n + 1)$: the Landau levels.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The potential is defined only up to a gauge transformation, and the equation must not care. The third example states
how the spinor transforms, in the convention of @def-emm-gauge-transformation.

::: {#exm-dq-gauge-invariance}
#### Gauge covariance

Under $A_\mu \to A_\mu - \partial_\mu\lambda$ and $\psi \to e^{iq\lambda}\psi$, $D_\mu\psi \to e^{iq\lambda}D_\mu\psi$, so
@eq-dq-minimal-coupling keeps its form and the current $\bar\psi\gamma^\mu\psi$ is unchanged. The kinetic momentum $\vec\pi$, not the
canonical $\vec p$, is the gauge-invariant velocity variable: $i[H, \vec x] = \vec\alpha$ still, and $\vec\pi$ appears in every
observable.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the Hamiltonian form from the covariant one. The signs of the lower-index potential are the
only trap.

::: {#exr-dq-coupled-hamiltonian}
#### The coupled Hamiltonian

Multiply @eq-dq-minimal-coupling by $\gamma^0$ and use $A_\mu = (\Phi, -\vec A)$ to derive @eq-dq-coupled-hamiltonian.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\gamma^0(i\gamma^0D_0 + i\gamma^kD_k - m)\psi = 0$ gives $iD_0\psi = -i\alpha_kD_k\psi + \beta m\psi$. With $D_0 = \partial_t + iq\Phi$ and
$D_k = \partial_k + iqA_k = \partial_k - iqA^k$: $i\partial_t\psi - q\Phi\psi = -i\alpha_k\partial_k\psi - q\alpha_kA^k\psi + \beta m\psi$, that is
$i\partial_t\psi = [\alpha_k(-i\partial_k - qA^k) + \beta m + q\Phi]\psi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The non-commutativity of the kinetic momenta is the magnetic field. The second exercise proves the commutator that
both the Landau levels and the factor $g = 2$ rest on.

::: {#exr-dq-pi-commutator}
#### Kinetic momenta do not commute

Show that $[\pi_i, \pi_j] = iq\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, and hence $\vec\pi \times \vec\pi = iq\vec B$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[\pi_i, \pi_j] = -q[p_i, A_j] - q[A_i, p_j] = -q(-i\partial_iA_j) + q(-i\partial_jA_i) = iq(\partial_iA_j - \partial_jA_i) =
iq\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Then $(\vec\pi \times \vec\pi)_k = \epsilon_{kij}\pi_i\pi_j = \tfrac12\epsilon_{kij}[\pi_i, \pi_j] = \tfrac12
iq\epsilon_{kij}\epsilon_{ijl}B_l = iqB_k$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The third exercise checks gauge covariance at the level of the Hamiltonian. It shows that a time-dependent gauge
transformation shifts the scalar potential as it should.

::: {#exr-dq-gauge-check}
#### Gauge covariance of the Hamiltonian

Let $\psi' = e^{iq\lambda}\psi$, $\Phi' = \Phi - \partial_t\lambda$, $\vec A' = \vec A + \nabla\lambda$. Show that if $\psi$ solves
@eq-dq-coupled-hamiltonian with $(\Phi, \vec A)$, then $\psi'$ solves it with $(\Phi', \vec A')$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\vec p - q\vec A')e^{iq\lambda}\psi = e^{iq\lambda}(\vec p + q\nabla\lambda - q\vec A - q\nabla\lambda)\psi = e^{iq\lambda}\vec\pi\psi$, and
$i\partial_t(e^{iq\lambda}\psi) = e^{iq\lambda}(i\partial_t - q\partial_t\lambda)\psi$. So $i\partial_t\psi' = e^{iq\lambda}[\vec\alpha\cdot\vec\pi + \beta m +
q\Phi - q\partial_t\lambda]\psi = [\vec\alpha\cdot\vec\pi' + \beta m + q\Phi']\psi'$. ($A_\mu \to A_\mu - \partial_\mu\lambda$ with $A_\mu = (\Phi,
-\vec A)$ is this transformation.)
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The equation that Pauli wrote for a non-relativistic particle with spin has a magnetic moment proportional to the spin
with an undetermined factor $g$. The definition below states it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-dq-pauli-equation}
#### Pauli equation

The **Pauli equation** for a particle of charge $q$, mass $m$ and spin one-half is
$$
i\partial_t\varphi = \Big(\frac{\vec\pi^{\,2}}{2m} - \vec\mu\cdot\vec B + q\Phi\Big)\varphi, \qquad \vec\mu = g\frac{q}{2m}\vec S, \quad
\vec S = \tfrac12\vec\sigma ,
$$ {#eq-dq-pauli}
for a two-component wave function $\varphi$; the dimensionless constant $g$ is the **gyromagnetic ratio**. For the
electron, $\vec\mu = -g\mu_B\vec S$ with the Bohr magneton $\mu_B = e/2m$ @svanberg2022spectroscopy [Sec. 2.3.2, eq. (2.12)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A magnetic moment in a field has an orientation energy, which splits the spin states. The first example evaluates the
splitting for a free electron in a field.

::: {#exm-dq-pauli-zeeman}
#### Spin in a magnetic field

For $\vec B = B\hat z$ the spin term is $-\mu_zB = g\mu_BBS_z$ for the electron, so spin up and spin down differ by $g\mu_BB$.
With $\mu_B = 5.788 \times 10^{-5}$ eV/T and $g = 2$, a field of $1$ T splits them by $1.16 \times 10^{-4}$ eV, a frequency of
$28.0$ GHz. @svanberg2022spectroscopy [Sec. 2.5.1, eq. (2.23)] records $g_s = 2$ "apart from a 0.1% correction due to quantum
electrodynamics".
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In an inhomogeneous field the orientation energy depends on position and exerts a force. The second example derives
it from the Pauli Hamiltonian by the Ehrenfest theorem.

::: {#exm-dq-stern-gerlach}
#### The Stern-Gerlach force

For a neutral particle with a magnetic moment ($q\Phi = 0$, $\vec\pi = \vec p$) the Heisenberg equation gives $\dot{\vec p} =
i[H, \vec p] = \nabla(\vec\mu\cdot\vec B)$. A field gradient $\partial_zB_z$ pushes the two spin states along $\pm z$ with force
$\pm\tfrac g2\frac{|q|}{2m}\partial_zB_z$: a beam splits in two, which is how the half-integer spin was first seen.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The spin precesses about the field at a rate set by $g$, and the orbit circles at the cyclotron rate. The third example
compares the two, which is the principle of the most precise measurement of $g$.

::: {#exm-dq-spin-precession}
#### Spin precession and cyclotron motion

From @eq-dq-pauli, $\dot{\vec S} = i[H, \vec S] = \vec\mu \times \vec B$, a precession with angular frequency $\omega_s =
g|q|B/2m$; the orbit has $\omega_c = |q|B/m$. For $g = 2$ the two coincide and the spin keeps its angle to the velocity. The
difference $\omega_a = \omega_s - \omega_c = (g/2 - 1)\omega_c$ is what @fan2023electron measure in a single-electron cyclotron:
$g/2 = 1.001\,159\,652\,180\,59(13)$, with the Dirac value $1$ as the first term of the prediction.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise solves the precession equation. It shows that only the component of the spin perpendicular to the
field moves.

::: {#exr-dq-precession}
#### Larmor precession

Show that $H = -\vec\mu\cdot\vec B$ with $\vec\mu = \gamma\vec S$ and constant $\vec B = B\hat z$ gives $\dot{\vec S} = \gamma\vec S \times
\vec B$, and solve it for $\langle\vec S\rangle(0) = \tfrac12\hat x$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$i[H, S_k] = -i\gamma B[S_z, S_k] = -i\gamma B\,i\epsilon_{zkl}S_l = \gamma B\epsilon_{zkl}S_l$, which is $\gamma(\vec S \times \vec B)_k =
\gamma\epsilon_{klz}S_lB$. So $\dot S_x = \gamma BS_y$, $\dot S_y = -\gamma BS_x$, $\dot S_z = 0$, and $\langle\vec S\rangle(t) =
\tfrac12(\cos\gamma Bt, -\sin\gamma Bt, 0)$: precession at $\omega = |\gamma|B$, with $\gamma = gq/2m$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In an atom the spin couples to the orbital angular momentum, and the magnetic moment of a level depends on how they
combine. The second exercise computes the Landé factors of the lowest hydrogen levels with Sage, using $g_s = 2$ and $g_l

1)} + g_s\frac{j(j + 1) + s(s + 1) - l(l + 1)}{2j(j + 1)}$. With Sage, evaluate it for $S_{1/2}$, $P_{1/2}$, $P_{3/2}$,
$D_{3/2}$, $D_{5/2}$ with $g_s = 2$, and again with the measured $g_s$ of @fan2023electron.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $g_s = 2$: $g_J = 2, \tfrac23, \tfrac43, \tfrac45, \tfrac65$. The measured $g_s$ shifts them in the third decimal:

{{< sage exr-dq-lande >}}

The anomaly frequency of @exm-dq-spin-precession is small and measurable. The third exercise evaluates the frequencies
for a realistic field. The numbers show why the anomaly, though tiny, is measured so precisely.

::: {#exr-dq-anomaly-frequency}
#### Cyclotron and anomaly frequencies

For an electron in $B = 5$ T, compute $\nu_c = eB/2\pi m$ and $\nu_a = (g/2 - 1)\nu_c$ with the value of @fan2023electron.
Compare $g/2 - 1$ with $\alpha/2\pi$, the first quantum correction.

1/137.036$, $\alpha/2\pi = 0.001\,161\,4$, which accounts for the anomaly to $0.15\%$; the remainder comes from higher orders
in $\alpha$ @fan2023electron [eq. (7)]. The Dirac equation alone gives $\nu_a = 0$.

The Dirac equation fixes $g$. The theorem below shows that its non-relativistic limit is the Pauli equation with exactly
$g = 2$, because of an identity of the Pauli matrices.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-dq-pauli-limit}
#### The non-relativistic limit

Write a solution of @eq-dq-coupled-hamiltonian in the Dirac representation as $\psi = e^{-imt}(\varphi, \chi)$. If the
fields and the kinetic energy are small compared with $m$, so that $|i\partial_t\chi - q\Phi\chi| \ll 2m|\chi|$, then
$$
\chi \approx \frac{\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi}{2m}\varphi ,
$$ {#eq-dq-small-component}
and $\varphi$ satisfies the Pauli equation @eq-dq-pauli with $g = 2$.

*Proof.* In the Dirac representation the two rows of @eq-dq-coupled-hamiltonian are $i\partial_t\varphi = \vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi\chi +
q\Phi\varphi$ and $i\partial_t\chi = \vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi\varphi + (q\Phi - 2m)\chi$, after removing the rest energy with
$e^{-imt}$. Under the hypothesis the second row gives @eq-dq-small-component, and the first becomes $i\partial_t\varphi =
[(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi)^2/2m + q\Phi]\varphi$. By $\sigma_i\sigma_j = \delta_{ij} + i\epsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$, $(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi)^2 =
\vec\pi^{\,2} + i\vec\sigma\cdot(\vec\pi \times \vec\pi) = \vec\pi^{\,2} - q\vec\sigma\cdot\vec B$ (@exr-dq-pi-commutator), and
$-\frac{q}{2m}\vec\sigma\cdot\vec B = -2\frac{q}{2m}\vec S\cdot\vec B$ is the term $-\vec\mu\cdot\vec B$ with $g = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The identity behind the theorem is worth seeing on its own. The first example states it, because it explains why the
factor two needs no input from experiment.

::: {#exm-dq-sigma-pi-square}
#### Where $g = 2$ comes from

$(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi)^2 = \vec\pi^{\,2} - q\vec\sigma\cdot\vec B$ holds for any potential. A Schrödinger particle with spin would
have the kinetic energy $\vec\pi^{\,2}/2m$, and one could add a magnetic moment with any $g$; but $(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi)^2/2m$, which
is equal to $\vec\pi^{\,2}/2m$ when $\vec B = 0$, comes with $g = 2$ built in. The Dirac equation forces this second form,
because its square must be the Klein-Gordon operator.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The small component is smaller by a factor of the velocity. The second example estimates it in hydrogen, where it
controls the size of the relativistic corrections.

::: {#exm-dq-small-components}
#### How small the small component is

For a free spinor, $|\chi|/|\varphi| = |\vec p|/(E + m) \approx v/2$ (@exm-dq-dirac-rep-spinors). In hydrogen the typical
velocity is $Z\alpha$, so $\chi \sim Z\alpha\varphi/2$ and its weight in the density is of order $(Z\alpha)^2/4 \approx 1.3 \times
10^{-5}$ for $Z = 1$: relativistic corrections are of relative order $(Z\alpha)^2$, which is why the fine structure is small.
For the exact ground state, $F/G = (1 - \gamma)/Z\alpha \approx Z\alpha/2$ (@exm-dq-ground-state).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In a uniform magnetic field the Dirac equation can be solved without approximation. The third example finds the exact
Landau levels of @fig-dq-landau and compares them with the Pauli levels.

::: {#exm-dq-landau}
#### Relativistic Landau levels

For $\Phi = 0$ and static $\vec B$, $H^2 = (\vec\alpha\cdot\vec\pi)^2 + m^2 = \operatorname{diag}((\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi)^2, (\vec\sigma\cdot
\vec\pi)^2) + m^2$. For $\vec B = B\hat z$, $(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi)^2 = \pi_x^2 + \pi_y^2 + p_z^2 - qB\sigma_3$ has eigenvalues
$|qB|(2n + 1) \mp |qB| + p_z^2$, so $E^2 = m^2 + p_z^2 + 2N|qB|$, $N = 0, 1, \dots$. For $|qB| \ll m^2$, $E \approx m +
p_z^2/2m + N|qB|/m$: the Pauli levels with $g = 2$, in which the spin energy $\pm|qB|/2m$ exactly fills the gap between orbital
levels.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise repeats the derivation of the theorem with care about the time dependence. It identifies the
hypothesis that is really needed.

::: {#exr-dq-pauli-derivation}
#### The derivation in detail

Derive the two rows used in the proof of @thm-dq-pauli-limit from @eq-dq-coupled-hamiltonian with $\beta =
\operatorname{diag}(1, -1)$ and $\alpha_k = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma_k \\ \sigma_k & 0\end{pmatrix}$, and show that the hypothesis holds
when the energy measured from $m$ and $q\Phi$ are small compared with $2m$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\psi = e^{-imt}(\varphi, \chi)$, $i\partial_t\psi = e^{-imt}(m + i\partial_t)(\varphi, \chi)$, and the Hamiltonian gives
$(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi\chi + m\varphi + q\Phi\varphi, \vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi\varphi - m\chi + q\Phi\chi)$; subtracting $m$ gives the two rows. If
$\chi$ oscillates like $e^{-i\epsilon t}$ with $|\epsilon| \ll m$ (the non-relativistic energy) and $|q\Phi| \ll m$, then
$(i\partial_t - q\Phi)\chi$ is of order $(\epsilon - q\Phi)\chi$, negligible against $2m\chi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

#### $(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi)^2$ by computer

With Sage, apply $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi$ twice to a two-component function $(f_1, f_2)(x, y, z)$ with $\vec A = (-By/2, Bx/2, 0)$ and
verify $(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi)^2 = \vec\pi^{\,2} - qB\sigma_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The cross terms $\sigma_x\sigma_y\pi_x\pi_y + \sigma_y\sigma_x\pi_y\pi_x = i\sigma_3[\pi_x, \pi_y] = i\sigma_3(iqB)$ produce the spin term:

{{< sage exr-dq-landau-sage >}}
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

The Dirac operator can be squared covariantly, and the magnetic moment appears as a term in the squared operator. The
third exercise performs this, which is how $g = 2$ is usually seen in field theory.

::: {#exr-dq-square-dirac}
#### Squaring the coupled Dirac operator

Show that $(\gamma^\mu D_\mu)^2 = D^\mu D_\mu + iqS^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}$, with $S^{\mu\nu} = \tfrac14[\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu]$ and $F_{\mu\nu} =
\partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu$, and that for a static magnetic field the extra term is $-q\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec B$. Deduce
that solutions satisfy $(D^\mu D_\mu + m^2 - q\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec B)\psi = 0$ when $\vec E = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu = \eta^{\mu\nu} + 2S^{\mu\nu}$, so $\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu D_\mu D_\nu = D^2 + S^{\mu\nu}[D_\mu, D_\nu] = D^2 +
iqS^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}$. With $S^{12} = -\tfrac{i}{2}\Sigma_3$ and $F_{12} = \partial_1A_2 - \partial_2A_1 = -B_3$ (lower indices
$A_k = -A^k$), the $(12)$ and $(21)$ terms give $iq\cdot2\cdot(-\tfrac{i}{2}\Sigma_3)(-B_3) = -q\Sigma_3B_3$, and cyclically. The Dirac
equation gives $(i\gamma^\mu D_\mu)^2\psi = m^2\psi$, i.e. $(D^\mu D_\mu + m^2 - q\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec B)\psi = 0$. Since $D_k = i\pi_k$,
$D^\mu D_\mu = \partial_t^2 + \vec\pi^{\,2}$, and for $\psi \propto e^{-iEt}$ this is $E^2 = m^2 + \vec\pi^{\,2} - q\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec B$, the $g =
2$ spectrum of @exm-dq-landau.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### The Foldy-Wouthuysen transformation

The Pauli equation is the first term of an expansion in $1/m$. To go further one must separate positive from negative
energies to higher order, by a unitary change of representation that removes the operators mixing upper and lower
components. For a free particle this can be done exactly, as the figure shows.

![The free Foldy-Wouthuysen transformation ($m = 1$). Left: the exact energy $\sqrt{p^2 + m^2}$ and the first two
corrections of its expansion, $m + p^2/2m$ and $-p^4/8m^3$. Right: the angle $\theta(p) = \tfrac12\arctan(p/m)$ of the exact
transformation $U = \exp(\beta\vec\alpha\cdot\hat p\,\theta)$, which tends to $\pi/4$ for ultrarelativistic momenta. Generated by
`figures/dq-foldy.sage`.](figures/dq-foldy.svg){#fig-dq-foldy width=95%}

The transformation acts on the two kinds of operators differently. The definition below names them, with respect to
$\beta$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-dq-even-odd}
#### Even operator

An operator on four-component wave functions is **even** if it commutes with $\beta$ and **odd** if it anticommutes with
$\beta$; every operator is the sum of its even part $\tfrac12(A + \beta A\beta)$ and its odd part $\tfrac12(A - \beta A\beta)$. In the
Dirac representation even operators are block diagonal and odd ones block off-diagonal. The coupled Hamiltonian
@eq-dq-coupled-hamiltonian is $H = \beta m + \mathcal{E} + \mathcal{O}$ with the even $\mathcal{E} = q\Phi$ and the odd $\mathcal{O} =
\vec\alpha\cdot\vec\pi$ @costella1995foldy [Sec. III].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Products of odd operators are even, as for signs. The first example uses this to show that the square of the odd part
of the Hamiltonian is the Pauli kinetic energy.

::: {#exm-dq-even-odd-free}
#### The square of the odd part

$\mathcal{O}^2 = (\vec\alpha\cdot\vec\pi)^2 = \operatorname{diag}((\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi)^2, (\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi)^2)$ is even, and
$\beta\mathcal{O} = -\mathcal{O}\beta$. The free Hamiltonian $\beta m + \vec\alpha\cdot\vec p$ has an even mass term and an odd kinetic term:
the kinetic term is what couples the large and small components, and removing it to a given order is the goal of the
transformation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The velocity operator of @exm-dq-velocity-operator is odd. The second example draws the consequence for its matrix
elements between energy eigenstates.

::: {#exm-dq-velocity-odd}
#### The velocity is odd

$\vec\alpha$ anticommutes with $\beta$, so in the Dirac representation it connects upper with lower components. For a free
particle it connects positive with negative energies as well, apart from its mean value $\vec p/H$: this is the origin of
the oscillating term in $\vec x(t)$ (@prp-dq-zitterbewegung). In the Foldy-Wouthuysen representation the velocity becomes
the even operator $\beta\vec p/E_p$ @costella1995foldy [eq. (2)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Chirality is odd in the Dirac representation. The third example notes this, which explains why the
non-relativistic limit hides chirality and the ultrarelativistic limit hides the rest energy.

::: {#exm-dq-gamma5-odd}
#### Chirality is odd

In the Dirac representation $\gamma_5 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ (@exr-fld-gamma-dirac-rep) anticommutes with
$\beta$: chirality mixes large and small components, and a slow particle, whose state is almost all large component, has
$\langle\gamma_5\rangle \approx 0$. The Weyl representation diagonalises $\gamma_5$ instead and makes $\beta$ odd, the natural choice
when $m$ is small (@prp-dq-chirality-helicity).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise establishes the multiplication table of even and odd operators. It is used at every step of the
expansion.

::: {#exr-dq-even-odd-products}
#### Products of even and odd operators

Show that the product of two even or two odd operators is even and that the product of an even and an odd one is odd.
Show that $\beta\mathcal{O}$ is odd and that $[\mathcal{O}, \beta] = 2\mathcal{O}\beta$ for odd $\mathcal{O}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $\beta A = \epsilon_AA\beta$ and $\beta B = \epsilon_BB\beta$ with signs $\epsilon$, then $\beta AB = \epsilon_AA\beta B = \epsilon_A\epsilon_BAB\beta$, so the parity
of a product is the product of parities. $\beta$ is even, so $\beta\mathcal{O}$ is odd. $[\mathcal{O}, \beta] = \mathcal{O}\beta - \beta\mathcal{O}
= 2\mathcal{O}\beta$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Hamiltonian $H = \alpha_3p + \beta m + V$, and check that they are block diagonal and block off-diagonal.

$\gamma^1$ and $\gamma_5$ are odd, $\Sigma_3$ is even, $\gamma^0\gamma_5$ is odd, and the Hamiltonian splits into $\beta m + V$ and $\alpha_3p$:

{{< sage exr-dq-even-odd-decomposition >}}

Whether an operator is even depends on the representation. The third exercise shows that the even part is not
preserved by a change of basis that does not commute with $\beta$.

::: {#exr-dq-even-odd-representation}
#### Even in one basis, odd in another

The change of basis $U$ of @exr-fld-gamma-dirac-rep maps the Weyl to the Dirac representation and maps $\beta_W = \gamma^0_W$ to
$\beta_D = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1)$. Show that "even" defined with $\beta_W$ in the Weyl representation and with $\beta_D$ in
the Dirac representation are the same notion, and that $\gamma_5$ is odd in both.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Evenness is defined by commutation with $\beta = \gamma^0$, a relation preserved by conjugation: $[A, \gamma^0] = 0$ iff $[UAU^{-1},
U\gamma^0U^{-1}] = 0$. So the notion is representation independent, though the block shape is not: in the Weyl
representation even operators are those commuting with $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, not block diagonal ones.
$\gamma_5$ anticommutes with $\gamma^0$ in any representation, so it is odd in both.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The transformation itself is a unitary change of representation, chosen to remove the odd operators. The definition
below states it, following the description of @costella1995foldy [Sec. III].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-dq-fw-transformation}
#### Foldy-Wouthuysen transformation

A **Foldy-Wouthuysen transformation** is a unitary $U = e^{iS}$, with $S$ Hermitian, such that the transformed Hamiltonian
$$
H' = e^{iS}(H - i\partial_t)e^{-iS}
$$ {#eq-dq-fw}
is even, exactly or to a given order in $1/m$. For the free Hamiltonian $H = \vec\alpha\cdot\vec p + \beta m$ the exact
transformation is $U = \exp(\beta\vec\alpha\cdot\hat p\,\theta)$ with $\tan2\theta = |\vec p|/m$, and it gives $H' = \beta\sqrt{\vec
p^{\,2} + m^2}$ @costella1995foldy [eq. (1)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The free transformation can be verified in a few lines because $\beta\vec\alpha\cdot\hat p$ squares to $-1$. The first
example carries it out.

::: {#exm-dq-fw-free}
#### The free transformation

$(\beta\vec\alpha\cdot\hat p)^2 = -\beta^2(\vec\alpha\cdot\hat p)^2 = -1$, so $U = \cos\theta + \beta\vec\alpha\cdot\hat p\sin\theta$. Since
$\beta\vec\alpha\cdot\hat p$ anticommutes with $H$, $UHU^\dagger = U^2H = (\cos2\theta + \beta\vec\alpha\cdot\hat p\sin2\theta)(\vec\alpha\cdot\vec p +
\beta m)$, whose odd part $\vec\alpha\cdot\hat p(|\vec p|\cos2\theta - m\sin2\theta)$ vanishes for $\tan2\theta = |\vec p|/m$, leaving
$\beta(m\cos2\theta + |\vec p|\sin2\theta) = \beta E_p$, the right panel of @fig-dq-foldy.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

With fields present there is no exact transformation, but one can remove the odd part order by order. The second
example performs the first step, which already gives the Pauli Hamiltonian.

::: {#exm-dq-fw-first-step}
#### The first step

With $S = -i\beta\mathcal{O}/2m$, $H' = H + i[S, H] + \tfrac{i^2}{2}[S, [S, H]] + \dots$ and $i[S, \beta m] = \tfrac{1}{2m}[\beta\mathcal{O},
\beta m] = -\mathcal{O}$ cancels the odd part, while $\tfrac{i^2}{2}[S, [S, \beta m]] = \beta\mathcal{O}^2/2m$ adds the even kinetic term:
$H' = \beta m + \beta\mathcal{O}^2/2m + \mathcal{E} + O(1/m)$-odd terms. The upper block $m + (\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi)^2/2m + q\Phi$ is
the Pauli Hamiltonian of @thm-dq-pauli-limit.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In the transformed representation the operators behave classically. The third example states the velocity, the
property that @costella1995foldy [Sec. III] single out.

::: {#exm-dq-fw-velocity}
#### Classical velocity

For $H' = \beta E_p$ the velocity is $i[H', \vec x] = \beta\vec p/E_p$, with a continuum of eigenvalues in $(-1, 1)$ and no
oscillation: in the Foldy-Wouthuysen representation $\vec x$ is the Newton-Wigner position, and spin and orbital angular
momentum are separately conserved. The price is that minimal coupling is no longer simple: the electron acquires a
magnetic moment and a Darwin term @costella1995foldy [Secs. IV-V].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

and find the $\theta$ that removes the odd part; check $UHU^\dagger = \beta\sqrt{p^2 + m^2}$ for $p = 3$, $m = 4$.

The odd part is $\alpha_3(p\cos2\theta - m\sin2\theta)$; for $p = 3$, $m = 4$, $\tan2\theta = 3/4$ gives $\cos2\theta = 4/5$, $\sin2\theta =
3/5$ and $H' = 5\beta$:

{{< sage exr-dq-fw-free-sage >}}

The angle of the free transformation is fixed by a single equation. The second exercise derives it and the limiting
behaviour shown in @fig-dq-foldy.

::: {#exr-dq-fw-angle}
#### The angle

From @exm-dq-fw-free, show that $\tan2\theta = |\vec p|/m$, that $\theta \approx |\vec p|/2m$ for slow particles, and that $\theta \to
\pi/4$ as $|\vec p| \to \infty$. What is $S$ to first order, and how does it compare with @exm-dq-fw-first-step?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The odd part vanishes when $|\vec p|\cos2\theta = m\sin2\theta$. For small $|\vec p|/m$, $2\theta \approx |\vec p|/m$; for large,
$2\theta \to \pi/2$. To first order $U \approx 1 + \beta\vec\alpha\cdot\vec p/2m = e^{iS}$ with $S = -i\beta\vec\alpha\cdot\vec p/2m$, which is the
$S = -i\beta\mathcal{O}/2m$ of the first step for $\vec A = 0$.
:::

The transformed position operator differs from $\vec x$, which is the content of the Newton-Wigner construction. The
third exercise computes the difference to first order.

::: {#exr-dq-fw-position}
#### The mean position

With $U \approx 1 + \beta\vec\alpha\cdot\vec p/2m$, show that $U^\dagger\vec xU \approx \vec x + \frac{i\beta\vec\alpha}{2m}$ to first order. Why does
this displacement, of the order of the Compton wavelength, matter for the Darwin term of @thm-dq-fw-hamiltonian?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$U^\dagger\vec xU \approx \vec x + [\vec x, \beta\vec\alpha\cdot\vec p]/2m = \vec x + \beta\alpha_k[\vec x, p_k]/2m = \vec x + i\beta\vec\alpha/2m$.
The operator that is "the position" in one representation is smeared over a distance $1/2m$ in the other; a potential
felt at the smeared position has, to second order, an extra term $\tfrac16\langle\delta x^2\rangle\nabla^2V$, which is the Darwin
term $\nabla^2V/8m^2$, the "charge radius" of @costella1995foldy [Sec. V].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

Carrying the transformation to second order in $1/m$ gives the Hamiltonian that contains the whole fine structure of
hydrogen. The theorem below states it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-dq-fw-hamiltonian}
#### The Foldy-Wouthuysen Hamiltonian

For $H = \beta m + \mathcal{E} + \mathcal{O}$ with $\mathcal{E} = q\Phi$ and $\mathcal{O} = \vec\alpha\cdot\vec\pi$, three successive
transformations of the form @eq-dq-fw give, up to terms of order $1/m^3$,
$$
H_{\mathrm{FW}} = \beta\Big(m + \frac{\mathcal{O}^2}{2m} - \frac{\mathcal{O}^4}{8m^3}\Big) + \mathcal{E} - \frac{1}{8m^2}[\mathcal{O},
[\mathcal{O}, \mathcal{E}]] - \frac{i}{8m^2}[\mathcal{O}, \dot{\mathcal{O}}] .
$$ {#eq-dq-fw-hamiltonian}
For a static potential energy $V(\vec x) = q\Phi$ and $\vec A = 0$ the upper block is
$$
H_{\mathrm{FW}}^{+} = m + \frac{\vec p^{\,2}}{2m} - \frac{\vec p^{\,4}}{8m^3} + V + \frac{1}{4m^2}\vec\sigma\cdot(\nabla V \times \vec p)
+ \frac{1}{8m^2}\nabla^2V ,
$$ {#eq-dq-fw-static}
and for a central $V(r)$ the spin-orbit term is $\frac{1}{2m^2r}\frac{dV}{dr}\vec S\cdot\vec L$. In the Coulomb case these are
the infinite-mass limit of the Breit potential of @eides2001hydrogen [eq. (35)].

*Proof sketch.* Each step uses $S = -i\beta\mathcal{O}_n/2m$ for the current odd part $\mathcal{O}_n$; expanding $e^{iS}He^{-iS}$ by the
Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff series and $e^{iS}(-i\partial_t)e^{-iS} = -i\partial_t - \dot S + \dots$, the odd terms of order $m^0$ and
$m^{-1}$ are removed and the even terms collected, which gives @eq-dq-fw-hamiltonian (@costella1995foldy [Sec. III] describe the
procedure and its validity). For the static case $[\mathcal{O}, V] = -i\vec\alpha\cdot\nabla V$ and $[\mathcal{O}, [\mathcal{O}, V]] =
-\nabla^2V - 2\vec\Sigma\cdot(\nabla V \times \vec p)$ (@exr-dq-double-commutator), and $\mathcal{O}^2 = \vec p^{\,2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For hydrogen the three corrections have names and sizes. The first example lists them, with the potential $V =
-Z\alpha/r$.

::: {#exm-dq-fw-hydrogen-terms}
#### The three corrections in hydrogen

With $V = -Z\alpha/r$: the **relativistic kinetic correction** $-\vec p^{\,4}/8m^3$; the **spin-orbit coupling**
$\frac{Z\alpha}{2m^2r^3}\vec S\cdot\vec L$, since $\frac1r\frac{dV}{dr} = Z\alpha/r^3$; and the **Darwin term** $\frac{1}{8m^2}\nabla^2V =
\frac{\pi Z\alpha}{2m^2}\delta^3(\vec x)$, since $\nabla^2(1/r) = -4\pi\delta^3$. Each is of order $m(Z\alpha)^4$, smaller than the Bohr
energies by $(Z\alpha)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Darwin term acts only at the nucleus and therefore only on $s$ states. The second example interprets it, with the
smearing of @exr-dq-fw-position.

::: {#exm-dq-darwin-smearing}
#### The Darwin term as smearing

If the electron feels the potential averaged over a sphere of radius $\delta$ around its position, the energy changes by
$\tfrac16\delta^2\nabla^2V$ to second order. With $\delta^2 = 3/4m^2$, a radius of the order of the Compton wavelength, this is the Darwin
term. For hydrogen it raises the $s$ levels by $\frac{\pi Z\alpha}{2m^2}|\psi_{n00}(0)|^2 = \frac{m(Z\alpha)^4}{2n^3}$
(@exr-dq-darwin-expectation), and leaves the others unchanged.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The three corrections depend on $l$ separately, but their sum depends only on $j$. The third example states the
result, which is the leading term of the exact spectrum of @thm-dq-dirac-levels.

::: {#exm-dq-fine-structure-first-order}
#### The fine structure to first order

In first-order perturbation theory (@prp-qm-first-order-shifts) the three corrections add to
$$
\Delta E_{nj} = -\frac{m(Z\alpha)^4}{2n^4}\Big(\frac{n}{j + \frac12} - \frac34\Big)
$$ {#eq-dq-fine-structure-first-order}
for every $l$ compatible with $j$ (@exr-dq-fine-structure-sum). The $l$-dependence of the kinetic and spin-orbit terms cancels
against the Darwin term for $l = 0$, which is why $2S_{1/2}$ and $2P_{1/2}$ stay degenerate.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise reduces the spin-orbit term for a central potential. It is the step from @eq-dq-fw-static to the
familiar $\vec S\cdot\vec L$ form.

::: {#exr-dq-spin-orbit-reduction}
#### The spin-orbit term

For $V = V(r)$ show that $\nabla V \times \vec p = \frac1r\frac{dV}{dr}\vec L$ and hence $\frac{1}{4m^2}\vec\sigma\cdot(\nabla V \times \vec p) =
\frac{1}{2m^2r}\frac{dV}{dr}\vec S\cdot\vec L$. Check the Coulomb case against @eides2001hydrogen [eq. (35)] at $M \to \infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\nabla V = V'(r)\vec x/r$, so $\nabla V \times \vec p = (V'/r)\vec x \times \vec p = (V'/r)\vec L$, the factor $V'/r$ commuting with
$\vec L$. With $\vec S = \vec\sigma/2$ the coefficient becomes $1/(2m^2)$. For $V = -Z\alpha/r$, $V'/r = Z\alpha/r^3$ and the term is
$\frac{Z\alpha}{4m^2r^3}\vec L\cdot\vec\sigma$, which is the last term of eq. (35) of @eides2001hydrogen at $M \to \infty$ (with $[\vec r
\times \vec p]\cdot\vec\sigma = \vec L\cdot\vec\sigma$).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Darwin term needs the value of the wave function at the origin. The second exercise computes it for the $s$
states, using the Laguerre form of the radial functions of @cini2023quantum [Sec. 11.2].

::: {#exr-dq-darwin-expectation}
#### The Darwin shift

Using $|\psi_{n00}(0)|^2 = (mZ\alpha)^3/\pi n^3$, show that the Darwin term shifts the $s$ levels by $m(Z\alpha)^4/2n^3$. Evaluate it
for the $1S$ and $2S$ levels of hydrogen in MHz.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{\pi Z\alpha}{2m^2}\cdot\frac{(mZ\alpha)^3}{\pi n^3} = \frac{m(Z\alpha)^4}{2n^3}$. With $m\alpha^4 = 1.449 \times 10^{-3}$ eV, i.e. $350.4$ GHz,
the shift is $175.2$ GHz for $1S$ and $21.9$ GHz for $2S$. The value at the origin follows from $R_{n0}(0) = 2(mZ\alpha/n)^{3/2}$ and
$Y_{00} = 1/\sqrt{4\pi}$, since $L^1_n(0) \neq 0$ in the radial function of @cini2023quantum [eq. (11.17)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The cancellation of @exm-dq-fine-structure-first-order is a computation with three expectation values. The third
exercise performs it with Sage for all levels with $n \leq 4$.

::: {#exr-dq-fine-structure-sum}
#### Summing the three corrections

Using $\langle1/r\rangle = mZ\alpha/n^2$, $\langle1/r^2\rangle = (mZ\alpha)^2/n^3(l + \frac12)$, $\langle1/r^3\rangle = (mZ\alpha)^3/n^3l(l +
\frac12)(l + 1)$ for $l \geq 1$, $\langle\vec p^{\,4}\rangle = 4m^2\langle(E_n - V)^2\rangle$ and $\vec S\cdot\vec L = \tfrac12[j(j + 1) - l(l + 1) -
\tfrac34]$, compute with Sage the sum of the three shifts for every $(n, l, j)$ with $n \leq 4$ and compare with
@eq-dq-fine-structure-first-order. ( $\langle1/r\rangle$ is @cini2023quantum [Sec. 11.3, Problem 3].)
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The kinetic term is $-\frac{m(Z\alpha)^4}{2n^4}(\frac{n}{l + 1/2} - \frac34)$, the spin-orbit term adds the $j$-dependence for $l
\geq 1$, the Darwin term supplies it for $l = 0$, and every case agrees with @eq-dq-fine-structure-first-order:

{{< sage exr-dq-fine-structure-sum >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The double commutator in the proof is where the spin-orbit and Darwin terms come from. The fourth exercise evaluates
it.

::: {#exr-dq-double-commutator}
#### The double commutator

For $\mathcal{O} = \vec\alpha\cdot\vec p$ and a function $V(\vec x)$, show that $[\mathcal{O}, V] = -i\vec\alpha\cdot\nabla V$ and
$[\mathcal{O}, [\mathcal{O}, V]] = -\nabla^2V - 2\vec\Sigma\cdot(\nabla V \times \vec p)$, using $\alpha_i\alpha_j = \delta_{ij} +
i\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k$. Deduce the last two terms of @eq-dq-fw-static.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[p_i, V] = -i\partial_iV$, so $[\mathcal{O}, V] = -i\alpha_i\partial_iV$. Then $[\alpha_jp_j, -i\alpha_i\partial_iV] = -i\alpha_j\alpha_i[p_j,
\partial_iV] - i[\alpha_j, \alpha_i](\partial_iV)p_j = -\alpha_j\alpha_i\partial_j\partial_iV - i\cdot2i\epsilon_{jik}\Sigma_k(\partial_iV)p_j$. The first
term is $-\nabla^2V$ by symmetry; the second is $2\epsilon_{jik}\Sigma_k\partial_iVp_j = -2\vec\Sigma\cdot(\nabla V \times \vec p)$. Multiplying
by $-1/8m^2$ gives $\frac{1}{8m^2}\nabla^2V + \frac{1}{4m^2}\vec\Sigma\cdot(\nabla V \times \vec p)$, the Darwin and spin-orbit terms.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
These exercises combine the Pauli limit with the Foldy-Wouthuysen expansion. The first compares the spin-orbit term with
the naive estimate from the magnetic field seen in the electron's rest frame.

::: {#exr-dq-thomas}
#### The Thomas factor

An electron moving with velocity $\vec v$ through an electric field $\vec E$ sees, to first order, the magnetic field $\vec B'
= -\vec v \times \vec E$. Show that $-\vec\mu\cdot\vec B'$ with $g = 2$ is $-\frac{q}{m^2}\vec S\cdot(\vec E \times \vec p)$, twice the
spin-orbit term of @thm-dq-fw-hamiltonian. (The factor $\tfrac12$ is Thomas precession, which the Dirac equation contains
automatically.)
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$-\vec\mu\cdot\vec B' = \frac{q}{m}\vec S\cdot(\vec v \times \vec E) = \frac{q}{m^2}\vec S\cdot(\vec p \times \vec E) = -\frac{q}{m^2}\vec
S\cdot(\vec E \times \vec p)$. With $\nabla V = -q\vec E$, the term of @eq-dq-fw-static is $\frac{1}{4m^2}\vec\sigma\cdot(-q\vec E \times \vec p) =
-\frac{q}{2m^2}\vec S\cdot(\vec E \times \vec p)$, half the naive value. The rest frame of the electron is accelerated, and the
rotation of its axes (Thomas precession) subtracts half the magnetic precession.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The exact Landau levels expand into the Pauli levels and a relativistic correction. The second exercise checks with
Sage that the correction is the $-\mathcal{O}^4/8m^3$ term of @eq-dq-fw-hamiltonian.

::: {#exr-dq-landau-expansion}
#### Landau levels to second order

Expand $E_N = \sqrt{m^2 + 2N|qB|}$ to second order in $|qB|$ with Sage, and show that the second-order term equals $-\langle\mathcal{O}^4
\rangle/8m^3$ with $\mathcal{O}^2 = (\vec\sigma\cdot\vec\pi)^2 = 2N|qB|$ on the level $N$ ($p_z = 0$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$E_N = m + N|qB|/m - N^2|qB|^2/2m^3 + \dots$, and $-(2N|qB|)^2/8m^3 = -N^2|qB|^2/2m^3$: on a Landau level the Foldy-Wouthuysen series is
the Taylor series of the square root:

{{< sage exr-dq-landau-expansion >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The spin-orbit constant of a level is what spectroscopists measure in alkali atoms. The third exercise computes it for
hydrogen from the Foldy-Wouthuysen Hamiltonian and compares with the splitting formula of @svanberg2022spectroscopy.

::: {#exr-dq-svanberg-zeta}
#### The spin-orbit constant

@svanberg2022spectroscopy [Sec. 2.3.2, eqs. (2.13)-(2.16)] writes the spin-orbit energy as $\zeta\,\vec l\cdot\vec s$ with splitting
$\Delta E = \zeta(l + \frac12)$. Compute $\zeta_{nl}$ for hydrogen from the spin-orbit term and show that $\Delta E$ for $2P$ is $m\alpha^4/32$,
equal to the full fine-structure splitting of @eq-dq-fine-structure-first-order. Why does the spin-orbit term alone give the whole
splitting between $2P_{1/2}$ and $2P_{3/2}$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\zeta_{nl} = \frac{Z\alpha}{2m^2}\langle r^{-3}\rangle = \frac{m(Z\alpha)^4}{2n^3l(l + \frac12)(l + 1)}$, so $\Delta E = \zeta(l + \tfrac12) =
\frac{m(Z\alpha)^4}{2n^3l(l + 1)}$, which for $n = 2$, $l = 1$, $Z = 1$ is $m\alpha^4/32 = 10.95$ GHz. From @eq-dq-fine-structure-first-order,
$\Delta E_{2,3/2} - \Delta E_{2,1/2} = \frac{m\alpha^4}{32}(2 - 1) = m\alpha^4/32$ as well. The kinetic and Darwin terms depend on $n$ and $l$
only, so they shift both $2P$ levels equally.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

## The Dirac hydrogen atom {#sec-dirac-hydrogen}

The Coulomb problem is one of the few in which the Dirac equation can be solved exactly, and its solution is the
benchmark against which the most precise measurements of atomic physics are compared. This part separates the equation
in spherical coordinates with the operator $K$ and the spinor spherical harmonics, reduces it to two coupled radial
equations, solves them, and compares the resulting spectrum with the measured fine structure and with the Lamb shift
that lies beyond it. The non-relativistic solution of @cini2023quantum [Chap. 11] is the model for the method, and the
spectrum and its corrections are those reviewed by @eides2001hydrogen [Secs. II and VII].

### Separation in spherical coordinates

In a central potential the orbital angular momentum $\vec L$ is not conserved (@exr-dq-helicity-commute), but $\vec J =
\vec L + \vec S$ and a sign that plays the role of $l$ are. The figure shows the result that the separation leads to,
the radial density of the ground state, which the relativistic equation pulls towards the nucleus.

![The radial density $G^2 + F^2$ of the Dirac ground state $1S_{1/2}$ in the potential $-Z\alpha/r$, in units of the Bohr radius
$a_Z = 1/mZ\alpha$, for $Z = 1$, $60$ and $92$, with the Schrödinger density $4\rho^2e^{-2\rho}$. For hydrogen the two are
indistinguishable; for heavy ions the relativistic state contracts and its density diverges weakly at the origin as $r^{2\gamma -
2}$ ($\gamma = \sqrt{1 - (Z\alpha)^2}$). Generated by `figures/dq-radial.sage`.](figures/dq-radial.svg){#fig-dq-radial
width=70%}

The operator that replaces $\vec L^2$ in the Dirac theory combines the spin-orbit operator with $\beta$. The definition
below introduces it and its eigenvalues.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-dq-k-operator}
#### Dirac's operator $K$

**Dirac's operator** is $K = \beta(\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec L + 1)$. It commutes with $\vec J$ and with every Hamiltonian
$\vec\alpha\cdot\vec p + \beta m + V(r)$ with a central potential, and $K^2 = \vec J^2 + \tfrac14$, so its eigenvalues are
$$
\kappa = \pm\big(j + \tfrac12\big), \qquad j = \tfrac12, \tfrac32, \dots
$$ {#eq-dq-kappa}
In the Dirac representation an eigenstate has upper components of orbital angular momentum $l = \kappa - 1$ if $\kappa > 0$ ($j =
l + \frac12$) and $l = -\kappa$ if $\kappa < 0$ ($j = l - \frac12$), and lower components of orbital angular momentum $l' = 2j - l$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The values of $\kappa$ label the familiar atomic states. The first example lists them for the lowest levels. The table is the dictionary between $\kappa$ and spectroscopic notation.

::: {#exm-dq-kappa-values}
#### The labels of the states

$\kappa = 1$: $S_{1/2}$ (upper $l = 0$, lower $l' = 1$). $\kappa = -1$: $P_{1/2}$ ($l = 1$, $l' = 0$). $\kappa = 2$: $P_{3/2}$ ($l = 1$,
$l' = 2$). $\kappa = -2$: $D_{3/2}$. $\kappa = 3$: $D_{5/2}$. The pairs $\pm\kappa$ have the same $j$ and opposite parity, since the parity
of the upper components is $(-1)^l$ (@exm-dq-parity-hydrogen). The spectroscopic label is that of the large component.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The square of $K$ is fixed by the total angular momentum, which is why its eigenvalues are half-odd integers in
absolute value. The second example derives this from the algebra of the Pauli matrices.

::: {#exm-dq-k-square}
#### The square of $K$

$(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L)^2 = \vec L^2 + i\vec\sigma\cdot(\vec L \times \vec L) = \vec L^2 - \vec\sigma\cdot\vec L$, using $\vec L \times \vec L =
i\vec L$. Hence $(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L + 1)^2 = \vec L^2 + \vec\sigma\cdot\vec L + 1 = (\vec L + \tfrac12\vec\sigma)^2 + \tfrac14 = \vec J^2 +
\tfrac14$, and since $\beta$ commutes with $\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec L$, $K^2 = \vec J^2 + \tfrac14$, with eigenvalues $j(j + 1) + \tfrac14 = (j +
\tfrac12)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In the non-relativistic limit $K$ reduces to an operator of the Pauli theory. The third example identifies it, showing
that $\kappa$ is the relativistic version of the spin-orbit quantum number.

::: {#exm-dq-k-nonrelativistic}
#### $K$ and the spin-orbit coupling

On the upper components $K = \vec\sigma\cdot\vec L + 1 = 2\vec S\cdot\vec L + 1$, so the spin-orbit term of @exm-dq-fw-hydrogen-terms is
$\frac{Z\alpha}{4m^2r^3}(K - 1)$ on them. For $j = l + \frac12$, $2\vec S\cdot\vec L = l$ and $\kappa = l + 1$; for $j = l - \frac12$, $2\vec S\cdot\vec L
= -(l + 1)$ and $\kappa = -l$. In the Dirac theory $K$, not $\vec L^2$, labels the states, and $l$ is recovered from $\kappa$ and the
choice of component.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise proves that $K$ is conserved. The key fact is that $\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec L + 1$ anticommutes with
$\vec\alpha\cdot\vec p$ while $\beta$ anticommutes with it too.

::: {#exr-dq-k-commutes}
#### $K$ commutes with $H$

Show that $\vec\alpha\cdot\vec p$ anticommutes with $\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec L + 1$ (use $\vec\alpha = \gamma_5\vec\Sigma$ in the Dirac representation
and $\{\vec\sigma\cdot\vec p, \vec\sigma\cdot\vec L + 1\} = 0$), and deduce $[K, H] = 0$ for $H = \vec\alpha\cdot\vec p + \beta m + V(r)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec p)(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L) = \vec p\cdot\vec L + i\vec\sigma\cdot(\vec p \times \vec L)$ and $(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L)(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec p)
= \vec L\cdot\vec p + i\vec\sigma\cdot(\vec L \times \vec p)$; $\vec p\cdot\vec L = \vec L\cdot\vec p = 0$ and $\vec p \times \vec L + \vec L \times
\vec p = 2i\vec p$, so the anticommutator is $-2\vec\sigma\cdot\vec p$, and adding $\{\vec\sigma\cdot\vec p, 1\} = 2\vec\sigma\cdot\vec p$ gives zero.
Since $\gamma_5$ commutes with $\vec\Sigma$, the same holds for $\vec\alpha\cdot\vec p = \gamma_5\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec p$. Then $K\vec\alpha\cdot\vec p = \beta(\vec\Sigma\cdot
\vec L + 1)\vec\alpha\cdot\vec p = -\beta\vec\alpha\cdot\vec p(\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec L + 1) = \vec\alpha\cdot\vec p\,K$; $\beta m$ and $V(r)$ commute with
$K$ because $\vec L$ commutes with functions of $r$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The eigenvalues of $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L$ on the coupled states follow from $\vec J^2$. The second exercise computes them,
which gives the relation between $\kappa$, $j$ and $l$.

::: {#exr-dq-k-eigenvalues}
#### Eigenvalues of $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L$

Show that on a state with $\vec L^2 = l(l + 1)$ and $\vec J^2 = j(j + 1)$, $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L = j(j + 1) - l(l + 1) - \tfrac34$, which is
$l$ for $j = l + \frac12$ and $-(l + 1)$ for $j = l - \frac12$. Deduce the relation between $\kappa$ and $l$ of @def-dq-k-operator.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\vec J^2 = \vec L^2 + \vec L\cdot\vec\sigma + \tfrac34$, so $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L = \vec J^2 - \vec L^2 - \tfrac34$. For $j = l + \frac12$: $(l +
\frac12)(l + \frac32) - l(l + 1) - \frac34 = l$; for $j = l - \frac12$: $(l - \frac12)(l + \frac12) - l(l + 1) - \frac34 = -l - 1$. With $\beta = +1$
on the upper components, $\kappa = l + 1$ or $\kappa = -l$, as stated.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The lower component has the other orbital angular momentum, because $\vec\sigma\cdot\hat r$ changes $l$ by one. The third
exercise shows this from parity.

::: {#exr-dq-lower-l}
#### The orbital angular momentum of the lower components

On the lower components $K = -(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L + 1)$. Show that if the upper components have $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L + 1 = \kappa$,
the lower ones have $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L + 1 = -\kappa$, and that this forces $l' = 2j - l$. Why must $l$ and $l'$ differ by one
for a parity eigenstate?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$K\psi = \kappa\psi$ means $(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L + 1)\varphi = \kappa\varphi$ and $-(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L + 1)\chi = \kappa\chi$. By
@exr-dq-k-eigenvalues, $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L + 1 = -\kappa$ with $\kappa = l + 1$ means $j = l' - \frac12$ with $l' = l + 1 = 2j - l$, and with
$\kappa = -l$ it means $j = l' + \frac12$ with $l' = l - 1 = 2j - l$. Parity acts as $\gamma^0 = \beta$ times $\vec x \to -\vec x$
(@def-dq-parity), giving $(-1)^l$ on the upper and $-(-1)^{l'}$ on the lower components; these agree only if $l$ and $l'$ have
opposite parity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The angular parts of the eigenstates are the eigenfunctions of $\vec J^2$, $J_z$ and $\vec L^2$ on two-component wave
functions. The definition below writes them with the Clebsch-Gordan coefficients of @eq-qm-clebsch-gordan.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-dq-spinor-harmonics}
#### Spinor spherical harmonic

For $l = 0, 1, \dots$, $j = l \pm \frac12 > 0$ and $m = -j, \dots, j$, the **spinor spherical harmonic** is the two-component
function on the sphere
$$
\Omega_{jlm} = \sum_{m_s = \pm1/2}\langle l, m - m_s; \tfrac12, m_s|j, m\rangle Y_l^{m - m_s}\chi_{m_s} ,
$$ {#eq-dq-spinor-harmonic}
with the spherical harmonics $Y_l^m$ of @def-spherical-harmonic and $\chi_{\pm1/2} = (1, 0), (0, 1)$. Explicitly, for $j = l +
\frac12$, $\Omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2l + 1}}\big(\sqrt{l + m + \frac12}\,Y_l^{m - 1/2}, \sqrt{l - m + \frac12}\,Y_l^{m + 1/2}\big)$, and for $j =
l - \frac12$, $\Omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2l + 1}}\big(-\sqrt{l - m + \frac12}\,Y_l^{m - 1/2}, \sqrt{l + m + \frac12}\,Y_l^{m + 1/2}\big)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For $l = 0$ only $j = \frac12$ occurs, and the harmonic is a constant spinor. The first example writes it.

::: {#exm-dq-harmonic-s}
#### The $s_{1/2}$ harmonics

$\Omega_{\frac12, 0, \frac12} = Y_0^0\chi_{1/2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}(1, 0)$ and $\Omega_{\frac12, 0, -\frac12} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}(0, 1)$: spin up
and spin down, with no angular dependence. They are eigenfunctions of $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L$ with eigenvalue $0 = l$, as
@exr-dq-k-eigenvalues requires for $j = l + \frac12$.
:::

The $p_{1/2}$ harmonics have angular dependence in each component, but not in their total density. The second example
computes them and finds that they are obtained from the $s_{1/2}$ ones by $\vec\sigma\cdot\hat r$.

::: {#exm-dq-harmonic-p}
#### The $p_{1/2}$ harmonics

With $Y_1^0 = \sqrt{3/4\pi}\cos\theta$ and $Y_1^1 = -\sqrt{3/8\pi}\sin\theta e^{i\phi}$, $\Omega_{\frac12, 1, \frac12} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}(-Y_1^0,
\sqrt2Y_1^1) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}(\cos\theta, \sin\theta e^{i\phi})$. Since $\vec\sigma\cdot\hat r(1, 0) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta e^{i\phi})$,
$\Omega_{\frac12, 1, \frac12} = -\vec\sigma\cdot\hat r\,\Omega_{\frac12, 0, \frac12}$: the operator $\sigma_r = \vec\sigma\cdot\hat r$ exchanges $l =
j \mp \frac12$ at fixed $j, m$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The angular densities of the spinor harmonics are those that spectroscopy sees in polarisation. The third example
finds that every $j = \frac12$ state is spherically symmetric.

::: {#exm-dq-angular-density}
#### Angular densities

$|\Omega_{\frac12, 1, \pm\frac12}|^2 = \frac{1}{4\pi}(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) = \frac{1}{4\pi}$: the $P_{1/2}$ states are isotropic like
the $S_{1/2}$ states, although their components are not. In contrast $|\Omega_{\frac32, 1, \frac32}|^2 = |Y_1^1|^2 = \frac{3}{8\pi}\sin^2\theta$:
the $P_{3/2}$, $m = \frac32$ state is concentrated near the equator. A $j = \frac12$ level has no quadrupole moment.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the eigenvalues of $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L$ on the explicit harmonics. It is done with Sage, using
the differential operators $L_\pm$, $L_z$ in spherical coordinates.

::: {#exr-dq-harmonic-eigen}
#### Eigenvalues on the explicit harmonics

With Sage, build $\Omega_{jlm}$ for $l = 1$ and all $j$, $m$ from @eq-dq-spinor-harmonic, apply $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L = \sigma_3L_z +
\tfrac12(\sigma_+L_- + \sigma_-L_+)$ with $L_z = -i\partial_\phi$, $L_\pm = e^{\pm i\phi}(\pm\partial_\theta + i\cot\theta\,\partial_\phi)$, and check the
eigenvalues $1$ for $j = \frac32$ and $-2$ for $j = \frac12$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Here $\sigma_\pm = \sigma_1 \pm i\sigma_2$, so $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L = \sigma_3L_z + \tfrac12(\sigma_+L_- + \sigma_-L_+)$. Sage's spherical harmonics include the
Condon-Shortley phase, matching @eq-dq-spinor-harmonic:

{{< sage exr-dq-harmonic-eigen >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The operator $\sigma_r$ is the angular part of $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec p$, and it maps each harmonic to its partner. The second
exercise proves its two key properties.

::: {#exr-dq-sigma-r}
#### The operator $\sigma_r$

Show that $\sigma_r = \vec\sigma\cdot\hat r$ satisfies $\sigma_r^2 = 1$ and anticommutes with $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L + 1$, and that $\vec\sigma\cdot\vec p
= \sigma_r\big(-i\partial_r + \frac{i}{r}\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L\big)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\vec\sigma\cdot\hat r)^2 = \hat r^2 = 1$. For the anticommutator, the computation of @exr-dq-k-commutes with $\vec p$ replaced by
$\hat r$ applies: $\hat r\cdot\vec L = 0$ and $\hat r \times \vec L + \vec L \times \hat r = 2i\hat r$ (both hold for any vector operator
built from $\vec x$). Finally $\sigma_r\vec\sigma\cdot\vec p = \hat r\cdot\vec p + i\vec\sigma\cdot(\hat r \times \vec p) = -i\partial_r + \frac{i}{r}\vec\sigma\cdot\vec L$,
and multiplying by $\sigma_r$ gives the formula.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The isotropy of the $j = \frac12$ states holds for every $l$. The third exercise proves it from the explicit formulas
and the addition theorem.

::: {#exr-dq-isotropic}
#### Isotropy of $j = \frac12$

Show that $\sum_m|\Omega_{jlm}|^2 = \frac{2j + 1}{4\pi}$ for any $j, l$, and that $|\Omega_{\frac12, l, m}|^2 = \frac{1}{4\pi}$ for each $m$
separately. (Hint: $\sigma_r$ is unitary and maps $\Omega_{\frac12, 0, m}$ to $-\Omega_{\frac12, 1, m}$.)
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Under a rotation the $\Omega_{jlm}$, $m = -j, \dots, j$, transform among themselves by a unitary matrix, so $\sum_m|\Omega_{jlm}|^2$ is
a rotation-invariant function on the sphere, hence a constant; each $\Omega_{jlm}$ has unit norm on the sphere, so the constant is
$(2j + 1)/4\pi$. For $j = \frac12$ the only values are $l = 0$, where $\Omega$ is constant, and $l = 1$, where $|\Omega_{\frac12, 1,
m}|^2 = |\sigma_r\Omega_{\frac12, 0, m}|^2 = |\Omega_{\frac12, 0, m}|^2 = \frac{1}{4\pi}$ pointwise, because $\sigma_r(\theta, \phi)$ is a unitary matrix at
each point.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
